newsitem.title: HAITI: Gold found in Haiti but peasants stop the drilling.
newsitem.headline: Gold found in Haiti but peasants stop the drilling.

text.p: Deep in the hills of the poorest country in the Americas a fortune in gold lies waiting, but to local farmers water is worth more than gold, officials said.

St. Genevieve Resources Ltd., a Canadian gold mining company that has been drilling near the northern port city of Cap-Haitien, has determined that the two small mines could yield at least $100 million dollars over 10 years.

But some 200 peasants who eke out a meagre living in the hills, armed with guns and machetes, stopped crews from working at the Morne Bossa site last month, demanding that a dam be built in the area to irrigate their fields.
"There were maybe 200 people from a local popular organisation and they had automatic weapons and machetes," St. Genevieve president Steve Lachapelle told Reuters. "We were scared."

The company had never experienced such an incident in its gold mining acquisitions in Africa, Cuba, the Dominican Republic or Russia. Lachapelle, a former colonel in the Canadian army, said he was not easily frightened but he has threatened to pull out of Haiti despite the substantial investment the company has already made.

"Haitian government officials have told me I won't pull out because we've already invested $6 million," he said. "But we are a high capital risk investment company and they don't understand that we can put $6 million in Haiti, leave, and concentrate somewhere else."
The company's net earnings last year more than doubled over 1995, at $19.2 million. At the end of fiscal year 1996, the company's total assets had reached $92.4 million.

Financial officials who support the Haitian government's plan to privatise nine state enterprises say it is critical that St. Genevieve not pull out. "If a high risk investor cannot make it Haiti, who will ever come invest here?" one official asked.

Leading the fight against privatisation in Haiti is former President Jean-Bertrand Aristide. Lachapelle said he was disillusioned with Aristide, whom he met in Washington when the former president was in exile after a 1991 military coup.

He said Aristide expressed support for his ideas for mining gold, copper and silver in Haiti at that point. But within days of the standoff at Morne Bossa Aristide broadcast a statement that Haiti was rich in gold, silver and copper and asked why foreigners should take it away.
"I was shocked by that statement," Lachapelle said. "I've always felt Aristide's goals were the right ones for Haiti."

Earnings from the gold mine would be split equally with the Haitian government, which does not have the technology or equipment needed to exploit the mines. St. Genevieve has already paid nearly $3 million in land concessions to the government and made a gift of a $200,000 mineral processing lab to Haiti's Mining Office.
The company has been negotiating with the farmers and was willing to strike a deal to help fund part of the dam. But in talks last weekend the peasants refused the deal.
